title: Exercise: convergence and cost
text:
Where this leads

Numerical differentiation (Part 7): forward, backward and central differences, the optimal step, Richardson extrapolation, and what to do with noisy measured OD data, where the “rounding” error is measurement noise and is far larger than \(\varepsilon\).
Solving nonlinear equations (Part 2): why bisection converges linearly and Newton quadratically, and how to stop an iteration.
Linear systems (Part 3): the \(O(n^3)\) cost of elimination, factor once and solve many times, and sparse storage and solvers for count matrices.
Large eigenvalue problems (Part 5, eigen-algorithms): PCA of 100 000 cells without forming the centred or the covariance matrix.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
About this lecture
Every numerical method answers two questions: how accurate is it, and how long does it take? Today we learn to measure both, with experiments rather than proofs.

Truncation error (from cutting off a Taylor series) against rounding error (from floating point): the first shrinks as the step h shrinks, the second grows.
Order of accuracy: error \approx C h^p, and how to read p as the slope of a log–log plot.
Convergence of iterations: linear (a fixed number of digits per step) against quadratic (digits double each step).
Cost: counting operations, big-O, timing code, reading the exponent from a doubling experiment, and memory.

Biology: the growth rate of a bacterial culture from an OD curve, and why a gene–gene correlation that takes a second for 100 genes takes hours for 20 000 genes × 100 000 cells.

This unit closes Part 1. Intro gave the three failure types, floating-point gave machine epsilon, error-conditioning gave relative error and cancellation. Here we put numbers on two things every later unit uses: how fast the error falls as we refine a method, and how fast the run time grows as the data grow. The habit we want: plot error against step size on log–log axes, and time against problem size on log–log axes, and read off the slope. Both slopes are predictions you can check.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Two questions about every method
Accuracy. Most numerical methods have a knob: a step size h, a number of iterations, a number of grid points.

How does the error change when I turn the knob? If I halve h, does the error halve? Quarter?
Can I turn the knob too far?

Cost. Most biological data sets grow: more genes, more cells, more time points.

If I double the number of genes, does the run time double? Quadruple? Go up eight-fold?
Will the answer fit in memory at all?

A single-cell RNA-seq experiment: 20 000 genes × 100 000 cells. A method tested on 100 genes can look instant and still be useless at full size.

Frame the whole lecture around these two knobs. The first half is about accuracy, with one running example (a numerical derivative). The second half is about cost, with gene-by-cell matrices. In both halves the tool is the same: a log–log plot and its slope. Ask the audience: if your pilot analysis on 100 genes ran in a second, how long for 20 000 genes? Most guess “200 seconds”. We will see why that guess can be off by a factor of a hundred or more.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Running example: growth rate from an OD curve
text:
Running example: growth rate from an OD curve
A bacterial culture follows a logistic curve, N(t) = \dfrac{K}{1 + (K/N_0 - 1)\,e^{-rt}}, with K = 1.2, N_0 = 0.05, r = 0.8 per hour.
The growth rate at time t is the slope N'(t). Approximate it by a forward difference: N'(t) \approx \frac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h}


The slope of the tangent (green) is what we want. The forward difference is the slope of the secant (dashed) through two points h apart. For large h they differ visibly. As h shrinks the secant turns into the tangent: that is the definition of the derivative from calculus. The question for today: how fast does it approach, and does it keep approaching on a computer? We use the logistic formula so that we know the exact answer, r N (1 - N/K), and can measure the error. With real data you would not; we come back to that.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
First try in R
K <- 1.2; N0 <- 0.05; r <- 0.8            # OD units, per hour
od <- function(t) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
t0 <- 3
exact <- r * od(t0) * (1 - od(t0) / K)    # logistic: N' = r N (1 - N/K)
h  <- 0.1
fd <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h
c(fd, exact, fd - exact)
# [1] 0.213147350 0.210259735 0.002887615

At t = 3 h the culture grows at 0.2103 OD units per hour; h = 0.1 h gives 0.2131.
Error \approx 0.003, about 1.4 % relative error. Not bad, but can we do better by shrinking h?


The exact derivative comes from the logistic differential equation, so we can compute the error exactly. The forward difference overestimates here because the curve is convex (bending upwards) at t = 3 h: the secant lies above the tangent. Make sure students see that the error is a number we can compute, and that it depends on h.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Make h smaller
h   <- c(0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001)
fd  <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h
err <- abs(fd - exact)
data.frame(h, fd, err)
#       h        fd          err
# 1 1e-01 0.2131473 2.887615e-03
# 2 1e-02 0.2105551 2.953551e-04
# 3 1e-03 0.2102893 2.959917e-05
# 4 1e-04 0.2102627 2.960551e-06

Each time h is divided by 10, the error is divided by 10.
The error is proportional to h: \text{err} \approx 0.0296\,h.


Read the table column by column. The leading digits of the error stay the same (2.9…) and the exponent drops by one each row. That is the signature of error proportional to h. The constant 0.0296 will turn out to be half the second derivative. Note that the code is vectorised over h: od() accepts a vector of times, so one line computes all four estimates.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Where “error \propto h” comes from: Taylor
Taylor’s theorem with remainder (from the intro unit): for some \xi between t and t+h, N(t+h) = N(t) + h\,N'(t) + \tfrac{h^2}{2}\,N''(\xi).
Subtract N(t), divide by h: \frac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h} = N'(t) + \underbrace{\tfrac{h}{2}\,N''(\xi)}_{\text{truncation error}}

Truncation error: the part of the Taylor series we cut off. It is there even with exact arithmetic.
Here N''(3) = 0.0592, so the error \approx \tfrac{0.0592}{2}\,h = 0.0296\,h. Exactly the constant in the table.


This is the one derivation of the lecture. It explains both the power of h (one, because one h was divided away from h^2) and the constant (half the second derivative). The second derivative of the logistic is r N’ (1 - 2N/K); at t = 3 that is 0.0592. Students do not need to compute it on the slide; the point is that the measured constant matches the theory. Truncation error is a property of the formula, not of the computer.

# 4 1e-10 0.210 1.47e-07
# 5 1e-11 0.210 5.70e-06
# 6 1e-12 0.210 3.90e-05
# 7 1e-13 0.210 4.28e-04
# 8 1e-14 0.205 4.87e-03
# 9 1e-15 0.111 9.92e-02

Below h \approx 10^{-8} the error grows again. At h = 10^{-15} the growth rate is off by half.


This is the failure. Truncation theory says the error should keep falling by ten per row. Instead it bottoms out near 1e-9 and then climbs, roughly by ten per row in the other direction. At h = 1e-15 the estimate is 0.111 instead of 0.210: a confident, wrong growth rate, with no warning from R. The culprit is the floating-point rounding we met in floating-point and the cancellation from error-conditioning.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Rounding error: \varepsilon / h

od(t0 + h) and od(t0) are each stored with a relative error up to \varepsilon \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}, i.e. an absolute error of about \varepsilon\,|N| \approx 10^{-16}.
For tiny h the two values agree in almost all digits: subtracting them is catastrophic cancellation (error-conditioning). The difference keeps the absolute error \approx \varepsilon |N| but loses the leading digits.
Dividing by h then amplifies it: \text{rounding error} \approx \frac{\varepsilon\,|N(t)|}{h}

.Machine$double.eps * od(t0) / 1e-12
# [1] 8.632834e-05
The table gave 3.9\times10^{-5} at h = 10^{-12}: the same size. This error grows as h shrinks.

This is a size estimate, not an exact formula: the rounding errors are effectively random, which is why the error column in the previous table was jagged rather than a clean power of ten. The factor 1/h is the key: the smaller the step, the more a fixed absolute error in the numerator is blown up. Link to .Machine$double.eps from floating-point. The same logic will appear whenever a method divides a small difference by a small number.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Total error: the V on a log–log plot
text:
Total error: the V on a log–log plot
\text{total error} \approx \underbrace{\tfrac{|N''|}{2}\,h}_{\text{truncation}} + \underbrace{\frac{\varepsilon\,|N|}{h}}_{\text{rounding}}

The two terms balance near h \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}; the best error is also \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon}: only about 8 of 16 digits survive.

On log–log axes each term is a straight line: slope +1 for truncation, slope -1 for rounding. The total error follows the larger of the two, giving a V. Setting the derivative of the sum to zero gives h* = sqrt(2 eps |N| / |N’‘|), here 5.4e-8, which for ordinary functions with N and N’’ of similar size is about sqrt(eps) = 1.5e-8 (shown in R as sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)). The best forward difference is accurate to about half the digits of a double. This V-plot is the most important picture of the lecture: every method with a step size has one.

title: Convergence and cost
Convergence and cost
section: Reading the order off a log–log plot
text:
Reading the order off a log–log plot
Take logs of \text{err} = C h^p: \quad \log_{10}\text{err} = \log_{10} C + p\,\log_{10} h. A straight line with slope p.
h   <- c(0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001)
err <- abs((od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h - exact)
log10(err[1] / err[2]) / log10(h[1] / h[2])   # slope from two points
# [1] 0.9901948
coef(lm(log10(err) ~ log10(h)))               # slope from all points
# (Intercept)    log10(h)
#  -1.5399748   0.9966565

Measured order \approx 1, as Taylor predicted. 10^{-1.54} = 0.029 \approx C.
Only fit the straight part. Points in the rounding regime would pull the slope towards -1.


Two ways to get the slope: from two points (rise over run in log10 units), or from a least-squares line with lm over several points. Both give about 1. Always look at the plot first and choose the range of h where the line is straight; fitting across the bottom of the V gives a meaningless number. This experiment, measure error for a range of steps and read off the slope, is the main check of every method in the course.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
A second-order formula, for contrast
The central difference \dfrac{N(t+h) - N(t-h)}{2h} is symmetric about t: the h^2 Taylor terms cancel and the error is O(h^2).


Slope 2: dividing h by 10 gains two digits. Best error \approx 10^{-12} at h \approx 10^{-5}.
The rounding side is the same as before. Full treatment in Part 7, Numerical differentiation.


We show the central difference only to see what a different order looks like on the plot: a steeper line on the right, the same rounding line on the left, so the V moves to larger h and lower error. Balancing C h^2 against eps/h gives h* ~ eps^(1/3) ~ 1e-5 and best error ~ eps^(2/3) ~ 1e-11. Derivations, the backward difference, Richardson extrapolation and noisy data are in Numerical differentiation (finite-differences, Part 7). Do not go further here.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Checking the order without the exact answer
text:
Checking the order without the exact answer
With real OD data you do not know N'(t). But if D(h) \approx N' + C h^p, then \frac{D(h) - D(h/2)}{D(h/2) - D(h/4)} \approx 2^p.
D <- function(h) (od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h
ratios <- function(h0) {
  d <- diff(sapply(h0 / 2^(0:5), D))   # successive differences
  d[-length(d)] / d[-1]                # should be 2^p = 2
}
ratios(0.1)
# [1] 1.961339 1.981418 1.990893 1.995493
ratios(3e-11)
# [1]  0.50 -0.50 -0.25  1.00
The check: ratios settle near 2^p → truncation regime, h is fine. Ratios jump around → you are in the rounding regime; use a larger h.

This is the practical check a student can run on their own method. The exact derivative cancels in the differences, so it does not need to be known. In the truncation regime the ratios approach 2 for a first-order method (4 for second order). Deep in the rounding regime they are noise, even negative. The same trick works for any method with a step size: quadrature, ODE solvers. Note that with measured OD values the noise is not 1e-16 but perhaps 1e-3, so the rounding regime starts at a far larger h; that is treated in finite-differences.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Convergence of iterations: digits per step
text:
Convergence of iterations: digits per step
Many methods do not have a step h but repeat a step until done. Two ways to find \sqrt{2}:

Halving (bisection): keep a bracket [1, 2] and halve it.
Newton: x_{k+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(x_k + 2/x_k\right), starting at x_0 = 1.

lo <- 1; hi <- 2; x <- 1                 # bracket [1, 2]; Newton start
for (k in 1:5) {
  mid <- (lo + hi) / 2                   # halving (bisection)
  if (mid^2 > 2) hi <- mid else lo <- mid
  x <- (x + 2 / x) / 2                   # Newton for x^2 = 2
  cat(k, signif(abs(mid - sqrt(2)), 2), signif(abs(x - sqrt(2)), 2), "\n")
}
# 1 0.086 0.086
# 2 0.16 0.0025
# 3 0.039 2.1e-06
# 4 0.023 1.6e-12
# 5 0.008 2.2e-16

Columns: step, error of the bisection midpoint, error of Newton. Bisection’s midpoint error wobbles, but its bracket halves every step, so the guaranteed error bound is 2^-k. Newton’s error goes 0.086, 0.0025, 2e-6, 2e-12, then machine precision: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step. Do not derive Newton here; that is Part 2. This slide only introduces the vocabulary.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Linear vs quadratic convergence





Linear: e_{k+1} \approx c\,e_k with c < 1. Bisection: c = \tfrac12, so about 0.3 digits per step; 16 digits take ~53 steps. Straight line on a log-y plot.
Quadratic: e_{k+1} \approx C\,e_k^2. Digits double each step: 1, 2, 5, 11, 16. A line curving downwards.
The order of convergence is the power: 1 for linear, 2 for quadratic.


Preview of Part 2: bisection, fixed-point iteration and Newton (Bisection and fixed-point iteration, Newton and secant methods).

For iterations the x-axis is the step number, not h, and we plot log error against linear k (a semilog plot). Linear convergence gives a straight line whose slope is log10(c); quadratic convergence gives a curve that falls faster and faster. Both stop at machine epsilon: you cannot get more than about 16 digits. log10(2) = 0.3 digits per step is why bisection is slow but steady. Part 2 shows when each method converges and how Newton can fail.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Cost: counting operations
Count the multiplications and additions (“floating-point operations”, flops) for vectors of length n and n\times n matrices:









Operation
R
Work
Flops




dot product \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf y
sum(x * y)

\approx 2n

A %*% x
n dot products
\approx 2n^2


matrix–matrix AB
A %*% B
n matrix–vector products
\approx 2n^3




For n = 20\,000: dot product 4\times10^4, matrix–vector 8\times10^8, matrix–matrix 1.6\times10^{13} flops.
A laptop does roughly 10^9–10^{10} simple flops per second (much more with an optimised library).


Build each count from the previous one: a matrix-vector product is n dot products of length n; a matrix-matrix product is n matrix-vector products. That is why the exponents go up one at a time. The 1e9 operations per second figure is a rough rule for one core doing simple arithmetic; optimised linear algebra libraries (BLAS) can be 10-100 times faster on many cores, but the exponent stays. Counting is approximate on purpose: we care about the leading power of n.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Big-O for cost: what doubling n does
text:
Big-O for cost: what doubling n does
Cost \approx C n^p, written O(n^p). Here n \to \infty and a smaller p is better. Doubling n multiplies the time by 2^p:





Cost
n \to 2n
100 \to 20\,000




O(n)
× 2
× 200


O(n^2)
× 4
× 40 000


O(n^3)
× 8
× 8 000 000






A matrix–matrix product: 2 ms at n = 100, 4.4 hours at n = 20\,000 (at 10^9 flops/s).

The right column is the “pilot to full study” factor: going from 100 to 20 000 is a factor 200 in n. For a linear method that is a factor 200 in time, for a quadratic one 40 000, for a cubic one 8 million. That is how a method that is instant on a pilot becomes useless at full scale. In the figure, read upwards along the green line at n = 20 000: the dot product is microseconds, the matrix-vector product about a second, the matrix-matrix product hours.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Biology: all-pairs gene correlation
A co-expression network needs the correlation of every pair of genes, each across all cells.

Number of pairs for n genes: n(n-1)/2. For 100 genes: 4 950. For 20 000 genes: ≈ 2×10⁸.
Each correlation is a dot product over m cells, O(m) work. Total: O(n^2 m).
For n = 20\,000, m = 100\,000: 2\times10^8 \times 10^5 \approx 2\times10^{13} multiply–adds.

Prediction: quadratic in genes, linear in cells. Going from 100 to 20 000 genes costs a factor 40 000.
Let us check that prediction by timing R’s cor().

This is the motivating calculation for the unit title. Write the count as (number of pairs) x (cost per pair). The pairs grow as n^2 because every gene meets every other gene. This is the same structure as a matrix product: the correlation matrix is (up to centring and scaling) X^T X, which costs n^2 m. Predictions like this can be wrong: the library may be cleverer than we think, or overheads may dominate. So we measure.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
A doubling experiment
set.seed(1)
cells <- 1000
genes <- c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000)
secs  <- numeric(length(genes))
for (i in seq_along(genes)) {
  X <- matrix(rpois(cells * genes[i], 2), nrow = cells)   # cells x genes
  secs[i] <- system.time(cor(X))["elapsed"]
}
data.frame(genes, secs, ratio = c(NA, secs[-1] / secs[-length(secs)]))
#   genes   secs    ratio
# 1   500  0.167       NA
# 2  1000  0.654 3.916168
# 3  2000  2.594 3.966361
# 4  4000 10.946 4.219738

system.time() returns seconds; "elapsed" is wall-clock time. Your numbers will differ; the ratio should not: × 4 per doubling, so O(n^2).


The doubling experiment is the simplest timing method: double n, and look at the ratio of times. A ratio near 2 means linear, near 4 quadratic, near 8 cubic. The data are simulated Poisson counts as a stand-in for a cells x genes count matrix. These timings were measured on a Linux server; a laptop may be faster or slower, but the ratio of about 4 should come out the same. Note that cor() correlates columns, so genes are columns here.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Log–log of time vs n: read the exponent, extrapolate
text:
Log–log of time vs n: read the exponent, extrapolate


coef(lm(log10(secs) ~ log10(genes))) gives slope 2.01: quadratic, as predicted.
Extrapolate: 20 000 genes ≈ 10.9 \times 5^2 \approx 270 s for 1000 cells, × 100 for 100 000 cells ≈ 7.6 hours. 100 genes × 100 000 cells: ≈ 0.7 s.


Same plot, same slope reading as for the error of the derivative, but now the slope is the exponent of the cost. Once you have the slope and one measured point you can predict the time at full size before you start the job. That is the payoff: you find out over coffee, not after a night of waiting, that the job needs a cluster, a faster algorithm, or fewer genes. A BLAS-based correlation (crossprod of the scaled matrix) is about 20 times faster on this machine, but it is still O(n^2 m): a better constant, the same exponent.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
When timing misleads
A timing is a measurement, with noise and systematic errors.

Too small: below ~0.1 s, start-up overhead and the clock resolution dominate. Times look flat in n, the slope comes out too low.
Multi-threaded libraries (BLAS, used by %*%, crossprod) use more cores as n grows, which also lowers the measured slope. Example: A %*% A here gave ratios × 2, × 3, × 6 for n = 500 \ldots 4000, not × 8.
Memory runs out: once the data no longer fit in RAM, times jump by orders of magnitude.

The check: time at least 3–4 sizes, increase n until each run takes ≥ 0.1 s and the doubling ratio settles. Then extrapolate.

This is the failure slide for timing. The classic mistake: time n = 10 and n = 20, see no difference, conclude the method is “fast”, and launch it at n = 20 000. The other classic: the slope from a multi-threaded library looks like 1.5 at moderate n, because more cores join in, and the extrapolation is too optimistic. Repeat timings and take the minimum or median if they are noisy. The numbers in the second bullet came from this machine with a 40-core OpenBLAS; on a laptop with R’s reference BLAS the ratio is much closer to 8.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Loops vs vectorised code
set.seed(1)
x <- runif(1e7); y <- runif(1e7)
dot_loop <- function(x, y) {
  s <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) s <- s + x[i] * y[i]
  s
}
system.time(dot_loop(x, y))["elapsed"]    # 0.555
system.time(sum(x * y))["elapsed"]        # 0.066
system.time(crossprod(x, y))["elapsed"]   # 0.032

All three are O(n). The constant differs: about 17× here; in plain Python loops it is more like 100×.
Vectorising changes C, never p. An O(n^2) method stays O(n^2) when vectorised.


Vectorised R functions (sum, x * y) run the loop in compiled C code; crossprod calls the BLAS library. The R loop interprets each iteration. Modern R compiles loops to byte code, so the gap is smaller than it used to be; in Python the gap between a for loop and numpy is typically 100 times or more (see the exercise). The point to land: vectorisation is worth a constant factor, often a large one, but it never changes the exponent. Choosing an algorithm with a lower exponent is what saves you at scale. The three sums also differ in the last digits, because they add in different orders.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Memory: 8 bytes per number
A double takes 8 bytes. A dense matrix with r rows and c columns takes 8rc bytes.
X <- matrix(0, nrow = 1000, ncol = 1000)
object.size(X)
# 8000216 bytes
20000 * 100000 * 8 / 1e9      # GB: genes x cells, dense
# [1] 16
20000^2 * 8 / 1e9             # GB: gene x gene correlation matrix
# [1] 3.2

object.size(): 10^6 entries × 8 bytes, plus a small header.
A full single-cell matrix as dense doubles needs 16 GB: a whole laptop’s memory, before any copy. R often makes copies.


Memory is the other cost, and often the one that bites first. Memory is O(rc) for a matrix; the correlation matrix is O(n^2) in the number of genes, 3.2 GB for 20 000 genes. Any operation that creates a modified copy (for example log-transforming the matrix) doubles the requirement. When the data do not fit, the operating system starts swapping to disk and the program slows down by orders of magnitude, or R stops with “cannot allocate vector of size …”.

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Sparsity: store only the non-zeros





Single-cell count matrices are typically 90 % zeros or more.
Sparse storage keeps only the non-zeros: value (8 bytes) + row index (4 bytes).
At 10 % non-zero: 16 GB → 2.4 GB. Work also scales with the number of non-zeros, not rc.


Full treatment: Part 3, Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse.

The sparse format here is compressed sparse column: for each non-zero, its value and its row index, plus one pointer per column. That is about 12 bytes per non-zero instead of 8 bytes per entry, so sparse storage wins whenever fewer than two thirds of the entries are non-zero, and wins massively at 5-10 % density. Operations such as a sparse matrix-vector product also only touch the non-zeros, so they cost O(number of non-zeros) instead of O(rc). Part 3 explains the storage formats and the solvers that exploit them.

title: Convergence and cost
section: Sparsity can be lost in one line
text:
Sparsity can be lost in one line
library(Matrix)                          # ships with R
set.seed(1)
S <- rsparsematrix(2000, 10000, density = 0.1,
                   rand.x = function(n) rpois(n, 2) + 1)  # genes x cells
D <- as.matrix(S)
c(dense = object.size(D), sparse = object.size(S)) / 1e6  # MB
#    dense   sparse
# 160.0002  24.0415
Sc <- S - rowMeans(S)                    # centre each gene ...
c(centred = object.size(Sc)) / 1e6       # ... and the zeros are gone
#  centred
# 160.0012

Centring subtracts the mean from every entry, so every zero becomes non-zero: the matrix is dense again. At full size: 2.4 GB → 16 GB.
The check: look at class() and object.size() after each step. Avoid centring the whole matrix; tools like PCA on sparse data centre implicitly.


The Matrix package comes with every R installation. rsparsematrix makes a random sparse matrix; we fill it with small counts as a stand-in for UMI counts. The failure is silent: R happily returns a dense matrix (class dgeMatrix) and the memory jumps six-fold here, or more at lower density. This is why single-cell tools scale and centre lazily, and why PCA on large single-cell data uses methods that never form the centred matrix (eigen-algorithms, Part 5).

title: Convergence and cost
text:
Summary

Truncation error comes from cutting off Taylor: forward difference error \approx \tfrac{|f''|}{2}h. Rounding error \approx \varepsilon|f|/h grows as h shrinks. Total error is a V; best h \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon}, only ~8 digits left.
Order of accuracy: error \approx C h^p = O(h^p). Read p as the slope of log(error) vs log(h), fitted on the straight part only. Without the exact answer: ratios of successive differences \approx 2^p.
Iterations: linear convergence gains a fixed number of digits per step; quadratic doubles the digits per step.
Cost: dot product O(n), matrix–vector O(n^2), matrix–matrix O(n^3), all-pairs correlation O(n^2 m). Doubling n multiplies time by 2^p.
Timing: system.time() at several sizes, slope of log(time) vs log(n), then extrapolate. Use sizes large enough to measure.
Memory: 8 bytes per double; 20 000 × 100 000 dense = 16 GB. Sparse storage keeps only non-zeros, until a centring step makes the matrix dense.


Two log–log plots carry the whole unit: error against h (slope = order of accuracy) and time against n (slope = cost exponent). Every later unit uses both. Next: Part 2, solving nonlinear equations, where linear and quadratic convergence come back with bisection and Newton.

title: Glossary
text: A running glossary of the numerical, mathematical and programming terms used in this course. Each entry links to the unit that treats it properly.

title: Glossary
text:
Part 1: Numbers on a computer

Why numerical analysis?
Numerical method — a finite sequence of arithmetic operations that approximates a mathematical answer. See Why numerical analysis?.
Rounding error — error from storing and computing with finitely many digits (about 16 significant digits for a double). Its relative size per operation is at most \(\varepsilon/2\).
Truncation error — error from stopping early: a finite sum, a finite step \(h\), finitely many iterations. It is there even with exact arithmetic.
Instability — an algorithm amplifying small errors, step after step.
Taylor polynomial \(P_n\) — the polynomial that matches \(f\) and its first \(n\) derivatives at a point.
Remainder term (Lagrange form) — \(R_n = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}\) for some \(\xi\) between \(a\) and \(x\); it bounds the error of the Taylor polynomial.
Convergence (of an optimiser) — the routine stopped because it no longer improves. It does not prove the answer is right.
Multistart — fitting from several starting values and keeping the best objective value.


How computers store numbers
Floating-point number — a number stored as \(\pm 1.f \times 2^e\) with a fixed number of significant bits. See How computers store numbers.
IEEE double — the 64-bit format: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 fraction bits; about 16 significant decimal digits.
Machine epsilon (\(\varepsilon\)) — the gap between 1 and the next double, \(2^{-52} \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}\). In R .Machine$double.eps, in Python np.finfo(float).eps.
Overflow — a result larger than about \(1.8\times10^{308}\); it becomes Inf.
Underflow — a result smaller than about \(4.9\times10^{-324}\) (the smallest subnormal); it becomes 0.
Subnormal number — a tiny double below \(2.2\times10^{-308}\), stored with reduced precision.
NaN — “not a number”: the result of an undefined operation such as 0/0 or Inf - Inf.
Integer overflow — exceeding \(2^{31}-1\) in a 32-bit integer. R gives NA; a numpy int32 silently wraps around to a negative number.
Log-likelihood — the sum of log-probabilities, used instead of the product of probabilities, which underflows.
Log-sum-exp — computes \(\log\sum_k e^{a_k}\) safely as \(m + \log\sum_k e^{a_k - m}\) with \(m = \max_k a_k\).
log1p / expm1 — accurate \(\log(1+x)\) and \(e^x - 1\) for small \(x\).


Error, conditioning and stability
Absolute error — \(|\hat x - x|\), in the units of \(x\). See Error, conditioning and stability.
Relative error — \(|\hat x - x| / |x|\). A relative error of about \(10^{-k}\) means about \(k\) correct significant digits.
Significant digits — the leading digits of a number that are correct; roughly \(-\log_{10}\) of the relative error.
Catastrophic cancellation — loss of correct digits when subtracting nearly equal numbers; costs about \(\log_{10}\big(|a| / |a-b|\big)\) digits.
Condition number (of a function) — \(\kappa = \left|\dfrac{x f'(x)}{f(x)}\right|\), the factor by which a problem amplifies relative errors in its input. You lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa\) digits.
Well-conditioned / ill-conditioned — \(\kappa\) near 1 / \(\kappa \gg 1\). Conditioning is a property of the problem.
Stability (of an algorithm) — an algorithm is stable if it loses no more accuracy than the problem’s conditioning explains. Stability is a property of the algorithm.
Backward error — the smallest relative change to the input for which the computed answer would be exact.
Backward stable — having backward error about \(\varepsilon\); then the forward error is at most about \(\kappa\,\varepsilon\).
One-pass / two-pass variance — \(\sum x^2/n - \bar x^2\) (unstable) vs \(\sum (x-\bar x)^2/n\) (centre first, stable).
Welford’s algorithm — a one-pass running update of mean and variance that avoids cancellation.


Convergence and cost
Order of accuracy — the power \(p\) in error \(\approx C h^p\). Halving \(h\) divides the error by \(2^p\); \(p\) is the slope of \(\log(\text{error})\) against \(\log h\). See Convergence and cost.
Big-O notation — \(O(g)\) means “at most a constant times \(g\)”: as \(h\to 0\) for errors, as \(n\to\infty\) for cost.
Linear convergence — \(e_{k+1} \approx c\, e_k\) with \(c<1\): a fixed number of digits gained per step.
Quadratic convergence — \(e_{k+1} \approx C e_k^2\): the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step.
Flop — one floating-point operation (an addition or a multiplication), the unit for counting cost.
Doubling experiment — timing code at \(n, 2n, 4n, \dots\); a time ratio of \(2^p\) per doubling reveals cost \(O(n^p)\).
Vectorisation — replacing an explicit loop by one call to compiled code. It changes the constant, not the exponent.
Sparse matrix — stores only the non-zero entries (value plus index): about 12 bytes per non-zero in compressed sparse column (CSC) format, against 8 bytes for every entry of a dense matrix.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
About this lecture
In How computers store numbers we saw that every double carries a tiny relative error, about 10^{-16}. Today: when does that tiny error become a large one, and whose fault is it, the problem’s or the method’s?

Absolute vs relative error, and why relative error counts correct digits.
Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting two nearly equal numbers.
The condition number \kappa of a problem: how much it amplifies relative errors in its input.
Stability of an algorithm: does it lose more digits than \kappa explains? Backward error in one slide.
Two cases: a well-behaved problem ruined by a bad formula (the one-pass variance), and a problem no formula can save (dose from a response near the plateau).


The thread of the whole lecture: an error in the output has two possible sources, and they need different cures. If the problem itself is sensitive (ill-conditioned), no algorithm helps; you change the experiment or the question. If the problem is fine but the algorithm is unstable, you change the formula. Students should leave able to tell which of the two they are looking at, and with two checks they can run. We use machine epsilon and “about 16 significant digits” from How computers store numbers without re-deriving them.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: A variance that comes out as zero
text:
A variance that comes out as zero
Cut sites from a CUT&RUN experiment pile up around one transcription factor footprint on chromosome 1, near position 240 000 000, spread over a few bp.
set.seed(3)
pos <- round(rnorm(1000, mean = 2.4e8, sd = 3))   # cut sites (bp)
n <- length(pos)
sum(pos^2) / n - mean(pos)^2        # textbook one-pass formula
# [1] 0
sum((pos - mean(pos))^2) / n        # centre first: two-pass
# [1] 8.986159

Same formula on paper, \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - \bar x^2 = \frac1n\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2.
On the computer one gives 0 (every read at the same base?), the other gives \approx 9\ \text{bp}^2.
No warning, no NaN. Which one is right, and why does the other fail?


Start with the failure. Both lines are the population variance (divide by n); they are algebraically identical, which every student has seen in a statistics course. The one-pass form is popular because it needs only one loop over the data (running sums of x and x^2), and it appears in old textbooks, spreadsheet formulas and streaming code. The answer 0 would mean all 1000 reads hit the same base, which is false. By the end of the lecture students can explain exactly why: it is cancellation, and the fix is to centre first. Genomic coordinates are a natural source of large numbers with a small spread; so are large counts and time stamps.

Absolute and relative error
For a true value x and an approximation \hat x:
\text{absolute error} = |\hat x - x|, \qquad
  \text{relative error} = \frac{|\hat x - x|}{|x|}.

The absolute errors differ by a factor 10^5; the relative errors are the same: both are 2 % off.
Relative error has no units and does not care about scale. It is the natural measure for anything that spans orders of magnitude (concentrations, counts, intensities).
Relative error fails when x = 0 or near it: then use absolute error.


Biologists already think in relative error (“within 2 %”) without naming it. Emphasise that a pipetting error of 1 microlitre is terrible for a 2 microlitre volume and irrelevant for a litre: that is relative error. The floating-point format is also built on relative error: from How computers store numbers, each stored number is within a relative error of about 1.1e-16 of the true one, whatever its size. The caveat about zero matters later, when we look at a difference that should be near zero.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Relative error counts correct digits
A relative error of about 10^{-k} means about k correct significant digits.
rel <- abs(3.1416 - pi) / pi
rel
# [1] 2.338435e-06
-log10(rel)                         # number of correct digits
# [1] 5.631075

3.1416 vs \pi = 3.14159265\ldots: five to six correct digits.
A double has \varepsilon \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}, so about 16 digits. That is the budget every computation starts with.
Today’s question: which operations spend that budget fast?


-log10 of the relative error is a handy digits counter, and we use it all lecture: in plots, in the exercise, and in the rule of thumb for the condition number. It is not an integer and need not be; 5.6 means “between 5 and 6 correct digits”. 16 digits sounds like a lot, and for a single operation it is more than any measurement in biology ever has (a very good measurement has 3 to 4). The danger is computations that throw away 10 or 16 digits at once.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Catastrophic cancellation
Subtract two numbers that agree in their leading digits:
a <- 1 + 1e-15                      # stored with relative error ~1e-16
print(a, digits = 17)
# [1] 1.0000000000000011
a - 1                               # should be 1e-15
# [1] 1.110223e-15
(a - 1 - 1e-15) / 1e-15             # relative error of the difference
# [1] 0.110223

The subtraction itself is exact. The damage was done when a was stored: an error in the 16th digit of a is now in the 1st digit of a - 1.
The leading digits cancel; what is left is mostly the old rounding error. That is catastrophic cancellation.


A common misconception is that the subtraction is the culprit. In floating point, subtracting two numbers within a factor of 2 of each other is exact. The problem is that the inputs carry errors (here from rounding 1 + 1e-15 to the nearest double), and subtraction keeps the absolute error while shrinking the result. So a relative error of 1e-16 becomes a relative error of 0.11. This is the most common way digits are lost in practice: in the variance formula, in differences of large measurements, in finite differences (Numerical differentiation), in the quadratic formula.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: Why: the error stays, the answer shrinks
text:
Why: the error stays, the answer shrinks


If a and b each carry absolute error \approx \varepsilon |a|, then a - b carries the same absolute error, so
\frac{\text{error}}{|a-b|} \approx \varepsilon\,\frac{|a|}{|a-b|}.

a = 1+d, b = 1: relative error \approx \varepsilon / d.
d = 10^{-8}: 8 digits left. d = 10^{-15}: barely 1.
Digits lost \approx \log_{10}\dfrac{|a|}{|a-b|}.





The plot is (1 + d) - 1 computed in R for d from 1e-16 to 1, with its relative error. It follows the dashed line epsilon/d: every factor of 10 by which a and b agree costs one digit. Points on the bottom edge are cases where the result happened to be exact. The factor |a|/|a - b| will come back in a moment under a new name: it is the condition number of subtraction.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Cancellation with measured data
Two near-identical spot intensities, each measured with about 1 % error: treated a = 2010, control b = 2000.
a <- 2010; b <- 2000
log2(a / b)                         # log2 fold change
# [1] 0.007195501
log2(1.01 * a / b)                  # a measured 1 % high
# [1] 0.02155079
log2(0.99 * a / b)                  # a measured 1 % low
# [1] -0.007304068

A 1 % error in a moves the log fold change by 200 %, even flips its sign.
Floating point is innocent here: 16 digits are plenty. The measurement error is amplified by the same factor |a|/|a-b| = 201.
The ratio a/b = 1.005 is still known to 1 %. What cannot be known is how far it is from 1.


Same mechanism, different source of the input error. In floating point the input error is 1e-16; in the lab it is 1 % or 10 %. The amplification factor is the same: |a|/|a - b|, here 2010/10 = 201. So the “change” between two nearly equal measurements is very uncertain, whatever software computes it. This is why small fold changes need replicates, and why a log fold change near zero with a large-looking relative error is not a computing bug. (If a ratio near 1 is given as 1 + small, computing its log is the log1p situation from How computers store numbers, which is about rounding, not measurement.)

Subtraction and \log are ill-conditioned near 1.
\sqrt{x} is always well-conditioned: it halves relative errors.





Work one entry on the board. For f(x) = x - 1: f’(x) = 1, so kappa = |x / (x - 1)|; at x = 1.001 that is 1.001 / 0.001 = 1001. This is exactly the cancellation factor |a|/|a - b| from before: cancellation is the ill-conditioning of subtraction. For log: f’ = 1/x, so x f’/f = 1/log x, huge near x = 1 where log x is near 0. For sqrt: f’ = 1/(2 sqrt x), so kappa = 1/2 everywhere. For exp: kappa = |x|, so exp(100) is moderately sensitive (a relative error of 1e-16 in 100 is an absolute error of 1e-14 in the exponent). Note that kappa depends on where you are, not only on f.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Measuring \kappa numerically
When f' is awkward, nudge the input and watch the output:
kappa_num <- function(f, x, h = 1e-7) {
  rel_out <- abs(f(x * (1 + h)) - f(x)) / abs(f(x))
  rel_out / h                       # relative change out / relative change in
}
kappa_num(function(x) x - 1, 1.001)
# [1] 1001
kappa_num(sqrt, 1.001)
# [1] 0.5
kappa_num(log, 1.001)
# [1] 1000.5

Matches the table. Works for any function you can evaluate, including a whole analysis pipeline.
h must be small but not tiny: h = 10^{-7} keeps cancellation inside kappa_num itself harmless (Numerical differentiation explains why).


This is the experimental condition number, and it is the check students can run on their own code: perturb an input by a small relative amount, see how much the output moves. If a 1e-7 nudge moves the output by 1e-2, kappa is around 1e5 and you should expect to lose 5 digits. The choice of h is itself a truncation-vs-rounding trade-off, which Convergence and cost and Numerical differentiation make precise; 1e-7 is a safe default for a smooth function in double precision.

Point out the asymmetry: double precision has so many digits that kappa = 1000 costs nothing of practical importance, but biological data have 2 to 3 digits, so kappa = 100 wipes them out. A stable algorithm loses at most about \log_{10}\kappa digits.

This table is the conceptual core. The output error depends on both: a stable algorithm on an ill-conditioned problem gives a poor answer, and so does an unstable algorithm on a well-conditioned problem, but for different reasons and with different cures. The typical mechanism of instability is that the algorithm routes the computation through a step that is ill-conditioned, such as subtracting two big nearly equal numbers, even though the final answer is not sensitive.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Backward error, in plain language
Instead of asking “how wrong is the answer?”, ask:

For which slightly different input is my answer exactly right?


That input change, as a relative size, is the backward error.
An algorithm is backward stable if its backward error is about \varepsilon: it solves exactly a problem within rounding distance of yours.
Then: forward error \lesssim \kappa \times backward error.

Example: (1 + 1e-15) - 1 gave 1.110223e-15. That is the exact answer for input 1 + 1.110223\times10^{-15}, which differs from the intended input by 1.1\times10^{-16}: backward error \approx \varepsilon. The 11 % forward error is all conditioning (\kappa \approx 10^{15}).

Backward error is how numerical analysts prove things about algorithms, but the idea is plain: if the answer is the exact answer to a question that differs from yours only by the rounding of the input, then the algorithm has done all anyone could ask. Whatever error remains is the problem’s sensitivity, kappa. The inequality forward error <= kappa x backward error is just the definition of kappa applied to the input change. Library routines (solve, lm, var) are designed to be backward stable. We do not compute backward errors in this course beyond this example; the term will reappear for linear systems (the residual) in Pivoting, norms and conditioning.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: Back to the variance: an unstable algorithm
text:
Back to the variance: an unstable algorithm
mean(pos)^2                         # the two terms being subtracted
# [1] 5.76e+16

\frac1n\sum x_i^2 and \bar x^2 are both \approx 5.76\times10^{16} and agree in their first 15–16 digits. Their difference, 9, is 10^{-16} of each term: catastrophic cancellation.
Near 5.76\times10^{16}, doubles are spaced 8 apart, so the one-pass answer can only be a multiple of 8: here 0.
Conditioning of the variance itself (relative nudges to the data): \kappa \approx 2\,\bar x/s \approx 1.6\times10^{8}, so up to 8 digits lost, 8 left.
One-pass loses about 2\log_{10}(\bar x/s) \approx 16: twice what the problem forces. That is instability.


The variance with large mean and small spread is moderately conditioned: if every data point is nudged by a relative 1e-16, the variance moves by a relative ~1e-8, because the absolute nudge (2.4e8 x 1e-16) is compared with a spread of 3 bp. (Here the positions are integers and are stored exactly, so even that loss does not occur.) The one-pass formula goes through two intermediate numbers of size mean^2 and subtracts them, which costs 2 log10(mean/sd) digits instead of log10(mean/sd). Spacing of doubles: 5.76e16 lies between 2^55 and 2^56, so the gap between neighbouring doubles is 2^(55-52) = 8.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: How many digits does one-pass lose?
text:
How many digits does one-pass lose?


Data with mean m and standard deviation 1. One-pass follows the grey line: 2 digits lost per factor 10 in m/s. Two-pass stays above the conditioning limit (green).
Counts around 10^8 with Poisson spread (s = 10^4): one-pass keeps only ~8 digits.


The experiment: 1000 standard-normal values shifted by m, for m from 1 to 1e9, variance computed both ways and compared with the exact answer. One-pass digits fall on the line 16 - 2 log10(m/s) and hit zero at m/s = 1e8. Two-pass keeps all 16 here, well above the green worst case the conditioning allows. For Poisson counts with mean 1e8, the sd is 1e4, so m/s = 1e4 and one-pass keeps about 8 digits: often enough for biology, but genomic positions, time stamps or sums of counts over many samples push m/s much higher.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
The fix: centre first
var(pos) * (n - 1) / n              # R's var() is two-pass (n - 1 scaling)
# [1] 8.986159
p0 <- pos - pos[1]                  # shift by any data value
sum(p0^2) / n - mean(p0)^2          # one-pass is now harmless
# [1] 8.986159

Variance is shift invariant. Subtracting a typical value first removes the large common part, so nothing big is left to cancel.
var() and numpy.var centre first. For streaming data use Welford’s running update, which also centres.
Check: recompute after shifting the data. A stable answer does not move.


Two lessons. First, use the library function: var() in R and numpy.var compute deviations from the mean first. Second, the shift check is a general diagnostic: if a quantity should be invariant under shifting or rescaling the data, compute it both ways; disagreement points to cancellation. Welford’s algorithm updates the mean and the sum of squared deviations one point at a time, so it works in one pass without the cancellation; we just name it. The n - 1 factor converts the sample variance that var() returns to the population version we used above.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Rewrite to avoid cancellation (1)
\sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x} for large x subtracts two nearly equal numbers. Multiply by the conjugate:
\sqrt{x+1} - \sqrt{x} = \frac{(x+1) - x}{\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{x}}.
x <- 1e15
sqrt(x + 1) - sqrt(x)               # cancels
# [1] 1.862645e-08
1 / (sqrt(x + 1) + sqrt(x))         # adds: no cancellation
# [1] 1.581139e-08

The problem is well-conditioned (\kappa \approx \tfrac12); the first formula is not stable. The rewrite turns a difference into a sum.


This is the standard rewrite pattern: when an expression subtracts two nearly equal quantities that you can write in closed form, look for an algebraic identity that removes the subtraction. Conjugates for square roots, log1p and expm1 for logs and exponentials near 0 (seen in How computers store numbers), trigonometric identities such as 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2). The rewritten version is correct to full precision; the first one has only 1 correct digit. At x = 1e12 the first version keeps about 5 digits; the exercise explores this.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Rewrite to avoid cancellation (2): binding
Protein P + ligand L, dissociation constant K_d, ligand depletion. The bound complex C is the small root of C^2 - S\,C + PL = 0, with S = P + L + K_d.
P <- 0.01; L <- 0.01; Kd <- 1e5      # nM: 10 pM each, Kd = 100 uM
S <- P + L + Kd
(S - sqrt(S^2 - 4 * P * L)) / 2          # textbook formula
# [1] 1.004082e-09
2 * P * L / (S + sqrt(S^2 - 4 * P * L))  # rewritten
# [1] 9.999998e-10

The textbook “-” root subtracts two numbers \approx 10^5 to get 10^{-9}: 2 correct digits. Rewrite: C = \dfrac{2PL}{S + \sqrt{S^2 - 4PL}}.
Sanity check: weak binding gives C \approx PL/K_d = 10^{-9} nM.


This is the quadratic-formula version of the same trick: multiply the small root by its conjugate. Since the product of the roots is PL, the small root is PL divided by the big root, and the big root has no cancellation. The quadratic appears whenever ligand depletion matters (tight binding, Morrison equation), and here a weak binder at low concentration makes the textbook formula lose 14 digits. The 0.4 % error looks harmless, but the same code with Kd = 1e6 is off by 42 %, and inside a fitting routine the error is noisy in the parameters. The asymptotic check C ~ PL/Kd is the kind of check to run on any formula: does it match a known limit?

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: An ill-conditioned problem: dose from response
text:
An ill-conditioned problem: dose from response


Response R = \dfrac{D}{K + D} (Michaelis–Menten shape, fraction of maximum). To infer the dose from a measured response, invert:
D = \frac{K R}{1 - R}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{1}{1 - R}.

R = 0.5: \kappa = 2.
R = 0.99: \kappa = 100. A 0.5 % error in R becomes a factor-3 range in D.





Derive kappa: f(R) = K R / (1 - R), f’(R) = K / (1 - R)^2, so R f’(R) / f(R) = 1 / (1 - R). Near the plateau, the curve is flat: a whole range of doses gives almost the same response, so reading the dose back is hopeless. This is the generic situation for any saturating curve: Hill functions, binding curves, standard curves of an ELISA or a qPCR assay at the top end. The figure shows the same response uncertainty (plus or minus 0.005) mapped to a narrow dose interval in the middle of the curve and a wide one near the plateau.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: No algorithm saves an ill-conditioned problem
text:
No algorithm saves an ill-conditioned problem
K <- 10                             # dose giving half response (uM)
dose <- function(R) K * R / (1 - R) # invert R = D / (K + D)
dose(c(0.495, 0.5, 0.505))
# [1]  9.80198 10.00000 10.20202
dose(c(0.985, 0.99, 0.995))
# [1]  656.6667  990.0000 1990.0000
kappa_num(dose, 0.99)
# [1] 100.001

The formula is exact and computed to 16 digits. The error comes from the data, amplified by \kappa.
Cures change the problem: dilute the sample into the steep part of the curve, measure more replicates, or report a lower bound (“D > 600 µM”).


Contrast with the variance: there, rewriting the formula fixed everything. Here, any formula gives the same spread, because the spread is in the inverse function itself. Higher precision arithmetic would not help either. The experimental cure is standard practice in the lab: dilute samples so they fall on the linear part of the standard curve. This is also what the Newton unit meets when solving a Hill equation for a dose: the root is well defined but poorly determined near the plateau.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
section: Teaser: the condition number of a matrix
text:
Teaser: the condition number of a matrix


Two dyes with overlapping spectra: unmixing solves A\mathbf x = \mathbf b.
A <- matrix(c(1,    0.95,
              0.95, 1   ), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
solve(A, c(1.95, 1.95))
# [1] 1 1
solve(A, c(1.96, 1.94))             # b off by 0.5 %
# [1] 1.2 0.8
kappa(A, exact = TRUE)
# [1] 39




0.5 % change in \mathbf b \to 20 % change in \mathbf x: amplified about 40 times.
Matrices have a condition number too (kappa()): Pivoting, norms and conditioning.


Only a teaser. The two equations are two nearly parallel lines; their intersection slides a long way when either line moves a little. The same rule applies: lose about log10(39), so 1.6 digits. With measured fluorescence (2 to 3 digits) that already matters. The matrix condition number, the norms it needs, and what it means for solving linear systems are the topic of Pivoting, norms and conditioning in Part 3. Note that kappa() without exact = TRUE returns a cheap estimate.

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Checklist: is my number trustworthy?

Estimate \kappa: by hand (|x f'/f|) or by nudging the inputs (kappa_num). Expect to lose \log_{10}\kappa digits of your data’s accuracy.
Look for subtractions of nearly equal numbers in your formula. Rewrite (conjugate, centring, log1p) or use a library routine.
Shift or rescale the data where the answer should not change; compare.
Check a limit you know (C \approx PL/K_d, variance \ge 0).
Impossible values (negative variance, probability > 1, a fold change of the wrong sign) are a symptom, not noise.


These are the habits we want. Step 1 separates the two failure types: if kappa times your input error is already large, stop worrying about the algorithm and think about the experiment. Steps 2 to 5 detect instability. The one-pass variance can even return a negative number for some data, which is impossible for a variance, so an impossible value is a red flag that should never be silenced with abs() or max(0, .).

title: Error, conditioning and stability
text:
Summary

Relative error |\hat x - x|/|x| counts correct digits: \approx -\log_{10} of it. Doubles start with about 16.
Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting nearly equal numbers keeps the absolute error and shrinks the result; lose \log_{10}(|a|/|a-b|) digits.
Condition number \kappa = |x f'(x)/f(x)|: how much the problem amplifies relative input errors. Lose about \log_{10}\kappa digits.
Stability: an algorithm is stable if it loses no more than \kappa explains; backward stable if its answer is exact for a nearby input.
Well-conditioned problem + unstable algorithm (one-pass variance): rewrite or centre. Ill-conditioned problem (dose near the plateau): no algorithm helps; change the measurement.
Next, Convergence and cost: truncation vs rounding error, and how fast methods converge.


Recap the two-source picture one last time: output error is roughly kappa times backward error. Kappa is fixed by the problem; backward error is what the algorithm controls. Convergence and cost adds the third ingredient, the truncation error of approximate methods, and how it trades off against rounding.

title: Exercise: how computers store numbers
text:
Background
A double (R’s numeric, Python’s float, numpy’s float64) stores a number as
\[x = \pm\, 1.f \times 2^{e}\]
in 64 bits: 1 sign bit, 11 bits for the exponent \(e\) (from \(-1022\) to \(1023\)) and 52 bits for the fraction \(f\). With the hidden leading 1 that is 53 significant bits, about 15–16 decimal digits.
Facts used below:

Binary. Whole numbers: divide by 2 repeatedly, read the remainders bottom-up. Fractions: multiply by 2 repeatedly, the integer parts are the bits. A fraction ends in binary only if its denominator is a power of 2; \(0.1 = 0.0\overline{0011}_2\) repeats forever, so it is rounded.
Machine epsilon \(\varepsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}\) is the gap between 1 and the next double. Each arithmetic operation returns the exact result rounded to the nearest double, with relative error at most \(\varepsilon/2\).
Gap near \(x\): \(2^{\lfloor \log_2|x| \rfloor - 52} \approx \varepsilon |x|\). The relative gap is constant; the absolute gap grows with \(|x|\).
Range. Largest double \(\approx 1.8\times10^{308}\) (above: Inf, overflow). Smallest normal double \(\approx 2.2\times10^{-308}\); subnormal numbers go down to \(4.9\times10^{-324}\) with fewer digits; below that: 0, underflow. exp(x) overflows for \(x > 709.8\) and underflows for \(x < -745\).
Special values. 1/0 = Inf, log(0) = -Inf, 0/0 = NaN, Inf - Inf = NaN. None of these gives an error or (in R) a warning.
Integers. Doubles store every whole number exactly up to \(2^{53}\approx 9.0\times10^{15}\). R’s integer type (5L) is 32 bits, maximum \(2^{31}-1 = 2\,147\,483\,647\); overflow gives NA.
Log-likelihoods. \(\log \prod_i p_i = \sum_i \log p_i\). To add probabilities stored as logs \(a_k = \log x_k\), use log-sum-exp: with \(m = \max_k a_k\), \[\log \sum_k e^{a_k} = m + \log \sum_k e^{a_k - m}.\]
Small arguments. log1p(x) \(= \log(1+x)\) and expm1(x) \(= e^x - 1\) stay accurate when \(|x| \ll 1\), where log(1 + x) and exp(x) - 1 lose digits.

The basic tools in both languages:

RPython


0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
# [1] FALSE
sprintf("%.20f", 0.1 + 0.2)            # show 20 decimals of the stored value
# [1] "0.30000000000000004441"
.Machine$double.eps                    # machine epsilon
# [1] 2.220446e-16
isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))      # compare with a tolerance
# [1] TRUE


import math
import numpy as np

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
# False
print(f"{0.1 + 0.2:.20f}")             # show 20 decimals of the stored value
# 0.30000000000000004441
print(np.finfo(float).eps)             # machine epsilon
# 2.220446049250313e-16
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))    # compare with a tolerance
# True

title: Exercise: how computers store numbers
text:
By hand
B1. Binary integers. (a) Convert 6, 13, 37 and 255 to binary. (b) Convert \(10110_2\) and \(1000000_2\) to decimal. (c) How many bits does it take to write 255? What is the largest whole number you can write with 8 bits?
B2. Binary fractions. (a) Convert 0.75, 0.3125 and 5.375 to binary. (b) Run the “multiply by 2” recipe on 0.2 for 8 steps. Show that the bits repeat and write 0.2 as a repeating binary fraction. (c) Without a computer: is 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 TRUE or FALSE in R? What about 0.1 + 0.7 == 0.8? Explain the difference.
B3. A toy floating-point system. Imagine a computer that stores numbers as \(1.f_1f_2f_3 \times 2^e\): 3 fraction bits, exponent \(e \in \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}\) (the picture on the “Floats are not evenly spaced” slide). (a) List all the numbers this system has in \([2, 4)\). (b) What is the gap between neighbouring numbers in \([1, 2)\)? In \([4, 8)\)? (c) Round 1.3, 5.3 and 6.2 to the nearest number in the system. Give the relative error of each. (d) What is machine epsilon for this system? What is the largest possible relative rounding error? (e) What is \(1 + 0.1\) in this system? And \(1 + 0.05\)? (f) What is the largest number in the system? What happens to \(7.5 + 4\)?
B4. The gap between doubles. Use \(\text{gap}(x) = 2^{\lfloor \log_2|x| \rfloor - 52}\). (a) Find the gap near \(x = 1\), \(1000\), \(0.001\), \(3.1\times10^9\) (a position in a concatenated human genome) and \(10^{16}\). First find the power of 2 just below each \(x\). (b) Is 1e16 + 1 == 1e16 TRUE or FALSE? (c) A genome browser stores the position \(3\,100\,000\,000.5\) (a point between two bases) as a double. Is it stored exactly? (d) For each \(x\) in (a), compute gap\((x)/x\). What do you notice?
B5. Spot the overflow and underflow. For each computation, say whether a double gives a normal number, Inf, 0 or NaN. Estimate the true value with powers of 10. (a) 1e200 * 1e200 (b) 1e-200 * 1e-200 (c) 0.01^200 (d) exp(1000) (e) factorial(200) (use \(200! \approx 7.9\times10^{374}\)) (f) 1e300 * 1e10 / 1e20 and 1e300 / 1e20 * 1e10 (g) The probability that 2000 reads all map correctly, if each maps correctly with probability 0.999: 0.999^2000. (Use \(\ln 0.999 \approx -0.001\).) (h) The likelihood of 2000 reads, each with probability \(10^{-3}\) under model 1: (1e-3)^2000. (i) The likelihood ratio of model 1 against model 2 (each read probability \(2\times10^{-3}\)): (1e-3)^2000 / (2e-3)^2000. What is the log of the true ratio?
B6. Log-sum-exp by hand. Use a calculator for exp and log (natural log). Useful values: \(e^{-1} = 0.3679\), \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\), \(e^{-12} = 6.14\times10^{-6}\), \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\). (a) Compute \(\log(e^{-500} + e^{-502})\) with the log-sum-exp formula. Then compute the two “posterior” weights \(e^{a_k} / \sum_j e^{a_j}\). (b) Compute \(\log(e^{2} + e^{2} + e^{2})\). Check against a simple rule. (c) Genotype calling. At one site, the log-probabilities \(\log P(\text{reads} \mid g) + \log P(g)\) for the genotypes AA, AB, BB are \(-1200\), \(-1198\) and \(-1210\). Compute \(\log P(\text{reads})\) and the posterior probability of each genotype. (d) Why does log(sum(exp(a))) fail for the numbers in (c)? (e) What would go wrong if you pulled out the smallest \(a_k\) instead of the largest, for \(a = (-1000, 0)\)?
B7. Small rates. (a) Use the Taylor polynomial \(\log(1+x) \approx x - x^2/2\) to compute \(\log(1 + 10^{-10})\) to 11 significant digits. (b) The computer first rounds \(1 + 10^{-10}\) to the nearest double (gap \(\varepsilon \approx 2.2\times10^{-16}\) near 1). How large can the error in the stored \(1 + x\) be, relative to \(x\)? About how many significant digits of \(\log(1 + 10^{-10})\) can log(1 + x) get right? (c) What does log(1 + 1e-17) return, and why? (d) A mutation rate is \(\mu = 10^{-9}\) per site per generation. Use \(e^{-\mu} \approx 1 - \mu + \mu^2/2\) to compute \(P(\text{at least one mutation}) = 1 - e^{-\mu}\) to 10 significant digits.
B8. Integers. (a) The human genome is about \(3.1\times10^9\) bp. Can a position on the concatenated genome be stored in R’s integer type? In a double? (b) A single-cell count matrix has 20 000 genes and 100 000 cells. Does the number of entries fit in a 32-bit integer? What about 30 000 genes? (c) Is \(2^{53} + 1\) a double? What does 2^53 + 1 - 2^53 return?

title: Exercise: how computers store numbers
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — decimal to binary (B1, B2)





Whole part: divide by 2 and keep the remainders; the last remainder is the first bit. Fraction part: multiply by 2; the integer part (0 or 1) is the next bit, then drop it and continue with the fraction. For 5.375, do 5 and 0.375 separately and join them with a binary point. To check, add up the place values (\(2^2, 2^1, 2^0, 2^{-1}, \dots\)).









Hint 2 — the toy system (B3)





Between \(2^e\) and \(2^{e+1}\) there are \(2^3 = 8\) numbers, evenly spaced with gap \(2^e/8\). Machine epsilon is the gap just above 1. To round, find the two neighbours and pick the closer one.









Hint 3 — the gap near x (B4)





Find the integer \(k\) with \(2^k \le |x| < 2^{k+1}\): \(2^9 = 512\), \(2^{10} = 1024\), \(2^{-10} \approx 0.000977\), \(2^{31} \approx 2.15\times10^9\), \(2^{53} \approx 9.0\times10^{15}\). The gap is \(2^{k-52}\). In code: 2^(floor(log2(abs(x))) - 52) in R; np.spacing(x) in Python.









Hint 4 — overflow and underflow (B5)





Work with powers of 10: a double is between about \(10^{-308}\) (or \(10^{-324}\) with subnormals) and \(10^{308}\). For powers, \(a^n = 10^{n \log_{10} a}\), or \(e^{n \ln a}\). Operations are done left to right, so the order in (f) matters. In (i), what is \(0/0\)?









Hint 5 — log-sum-exp (B6, C6)





Subtract the largest \(a_k\) from every \(a_k\), exponentiate (now the largest term is \(e^0 = 1\)), add, take the log, and add the largest \(a_k\) back. The posterior weights are \(e^{a_k - \text{LSE}}\), where LSE is the log-sum-exp; they add up to 1. In R, max, exp, sum, log; in Python, np.max, np.exp, np.sum, np.log, or scipy.special.logsumexp.









Hint 6 — comparing with a tolerance (C1, C3)





R: all.equal(a, b) returns TRUE or a description of the difference, so use isTRUE(all.equal(a, b)) in an if. Python: math.isclose(a, b) for single numbers, np.isclose(a, b) for arrays. For your own near, use abs and pmax (R) or np.abs and np.maximum (Python). See sprintf (R) or an f-string f"{x:.20f}" (Python) to print digits.









Hint 7 — limits of the number system (C2, C4)





R: .Machine has double.eps, double.xmax, double.xmin and integer.max. Python: np.finfo(float) has .eps, .max, .tiny, .smallest_subnormal; np.iinfo(np.int32) has .max. Convert integers to doubles with as.numeric() (R) or .astype(np.float64) (Python). Check results with is.finite / np.isfinite.









Hint 8 — log-likelihoods (C5)





Use sapply(lambda, function(l) ...) in R or a list comprehension in Python to loop over the grid. which.max (R) and np.argmax (Python) return the first maximum, so if every value is 0 they return the first grid point.

Solution





B1. (a) \(6\): \(6/2 = 3\) r \(0\), \(3/2 = 1\) r \(1\), \(1/2 = 0\) r \(1\) → \(110_2\). \(13 = 1101_2\) (lecture). \(37 = 32 + 4 + 1 = 100101_2\). \(255 = 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 11111111_2\). (b) \(10110_2 = 16 + 4 + 2 = 22\). \(1000000_2 = 2^6 = 64\). (c) 8 bits; \(11111111_2 = 2^8 - 1 = 255\) is the largest. In general \(n\) bits hold \(0\) to \(2^n - 1\), which is why a 32-bit signed integer (one bit for the sign) stops at \(2^{31} - 1\).
B2. (a) \(0.75\): \(1.5\) → 1, \(1.0\) → 1, so \(0.11_2\). \(0.3125\): \(0.625\) → 0, \(1.25\) → 1, \(0.5\) → 0, \(1.0\) → 1, so \(0.0101_2\) (\(= \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16}\)). \(5.375 = 101_2 + 0.011_2 = 101.011_2\). (b) \(0.2 \to 0.4\) (0) \(\to 0.8\) (0) \(\to 1.6\) (1) \(\to 1.2\) (1) \(\to 0.4\) (0) \(\to 0.8\) (0) \(\to 1.6\) (1) \(\to 1.2\) (1). After four steps we are back at 0.4, so the block \(0011\) repeats: \(0.2 = 0.\overline{0011}_2\). (c) 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 is TRUE: all three are exact in binary and the sum is exact. 0.1 + 0.7 == 0.8 is FALSE (try it): none of the three is exact, and the rounded sum need not land on the rounded 0.8.
B3. (a) The gap in \([2, 4)\) is \(2/8 = 0.25\): \(2, 2.25, 2.5, 2.75, 3, 3.25, 3.5, 3.75\). (b) \([1, 2)\): gap \(1/8 = 0.125\). \([4, 8)\): gap \(4/8 = 0.5\). (c) \(1.3\) lies between \(1.25\) and \(1.375\); it is \(0.05\) from \(1.25\), so it rounds to \(1.25\) (relative error \(0.05/1.3 = 3.8\%\)). \(5.3\) lies between \(5.0\) and \(5.5\); it is \(0.2\) from \(5.5\), so \(5.5\) (error \(0.2/5.3 = 3.8\%\)). \(6.2\) lies between \(6.0\) and \(6.5\); it rounds to \(6.0\) (error \(0.2/6.2 = 3.2\%\)). (d) \(\varepsilon_\text{toy} = 1/8 = 0.125\). The worst rounding error is half a gap, so the relative error is at most \(\varepsilon_\text{toy}/2 = 6.25\%\). All three in (c) are below that. (e) \(1.1\) lies between \(1\) and \(1.125\) and is closer to \(1.125\), so \(1 + 0.1 = 1.125\). \(1.05\) is closer to \(1\), so \(1 + 0.05 = 1\): the 0.05 is lost completely. Any \(x\) below \(\varepsilon_\text{toy}/2 = 1/16\) vanishes when added to 1. (f) Largest: \(1.111_2 \times 2^2 = 1.875 \times 4 = 7.5\). \(7.5 + 4 = 11.5\) is beyond the range: overflow. (An IEEE system would return Inf.)

Near \(10^{16}\) the gap is 2, so the neighbours of \(10^{16}\) are \(10^{16} \pm 2\). \(10^{16} + 1\) is exactly halfway; IEEE breaks ties towards the neighbour whose last bit is 0 (“round half to even”), which here is \(10^{16}\) itself. So 1e16 + 1 == 1e16 is TRUE (C2 confirms).
Yes. The gap near \(3.1\times10^9\) is \(2^{-21}\), and \(0.5 = 2^{-1}\) is a whole multiple of it, so \(3\,100\,000\,000.5\) is a double. (Positions with up to 6 decimals would be rounded, at the 7th decimal.)
gap\(/x\) is always between \(1.1\times10^{-16}\) and \(2.2\times10^{-16}\): the relative gap is the same for every size of \(x\), between \(\varepsilon/2\) and \(\varepsilon\).

B5. (a) \(10^{400}\) → Inf (overflow). (b) \(10^{-400}\) → 0 (underflow; below even the subnormals). (c) \(0.01^{200} = 10^{-400}\) → 0. (d) \(e^{1000} \approx 10^{434}\) → Inf (above 709.8). (e) \(7.9\times10^{374}\) → Inf. (f) Left to right: \(10^{300}\cdot10^{10} = 10^{310}\) → Inf, and Inf / 1e20 is still Inf. The other order: \(10^{300}/10^{20} = 10^{280}\), times \(10^{10}\) is \(10^{290}\), a normal number. The order of operations decides whether an intermediate result overflows. (g) \(0.999^{2000} = e^{2000 \ln 0.999} \approx e^{-2} \approx 0.135\), a normal number. Multiplying many numbers close to 1 is harmless. (h) \(10^{-6000}\) → 0. (i) Both are 0, so the ratio is \(0/0\) = NaN. The true ratio is \((1/2)^{2000}\); its log is \(2000 \ln(1/2) = -1386.3\). (The ratio itself, \(10^{-602}\), would underflow too; the log is the only form a computer can hold.) On the log scale: \(2000(\ln 10^{-3} - \ln (2\times10^{-3})) = -2000 \ln 2\).
B6. (a) \(m = -500\). \(e^{0} + e^{-2} = 1 + 0.1353 = 1.1353\); \(\ln 1.1353 = 0.1269\). So \(\log(e^{-500} + e^{-502}) = -500 + 0.1269 = -499.873\). Weights: \(e^{0}/1.1353 = 0.881\) and \(e^{-2}/1.1353 = 0.119\); they add up to 1. (b) \(m = 2\); \(1 + 1 + 1 = 3\); result \(2 + \ln 3 = 3.0986\). Rule: \(\log(n\,e^{a}) = a + \log n\). (c) \(m = -1198\) (AB). \(e^{-2} + e^{0} + e^{-12} = 0.13534 + 1 + 0.00000614 = 1.13534\); \(\ln 1.13534 = 0.12693\). So \(\log P(\text{reads}) = -1198 + 0.12693 = -1197.873\). Posteriors: AA \(0.13534/1.13534 = 0.119\), AB \(1/1.13534 = 0.881\), BB \(6.14\times10^{-6}/1.13534 = 5.4\times10^{-6}\). (d) \(e^{-1198}\) is far below \(e^{-745}\), so every exp(a) underflows to 0, the sum is 0, and \(\log 0 = -\infty\). (e) With \(m = -1000\), the terms are \(e^{0} = 1\) and \(e^{1000}\), which overflows to Inf, so the result is Inf. Pulling out the largest term guarantees every exponent is \(\le 0\).
B7. (a) \(10^{-10} - \tfrac12 10^{-20} = 9.9999999995\times10^{-11}\) (the next Taylor term, \(x^3/3\), is \(3\times10^{-31}\), far too small to matter). (b) The stored \(1 + x\) can be off by up to half a gap, \(1.1\times10^{-16}\). Relative to \(x = 10^{-10}\) that is \(1.1\times10^{-6}\), so only about 6–7 significant digits of \(x\) (and so of \(\log(1+x)\)) survive. R gives log(1 + 1e-10) \(= 1.000000082690371\times10^{-10}\): correct to 7 digits. (c) \(10^{-17} < \varepsilon/2\), so \(1 + 10^{-17}\) rounds to exactly 1 and log(1) returns 0: 100% error. log1p(1e-17) returns 1e-17. (d) \(1 - (1 - \mu + \mu^2/2) = \mu - \mu^2/2 = 10^{-9} - 5\times10^{-19} = 9.999999995\times10^{-10}\). This is what -expm1(-mu) returns on the slide; the naive 1 - exp(-mu) gives \(9.99999971718069\times10^{-10}\), wrong from the 8th digit.
B8. (a) Not as an R integer: \(3.1\times10^9 > 2^{31} - 1 \approx 2.147\times10^9\). As a double, yes: every whole number up to \(9\times10^{15}\) is exact. (b) \(20\,000 \times 100\,000 = 2\times10^9 < 2.147\times10^9\): it fits, barely. \(30\,000 \times 100\,000 = 3\times10^9\) does not. This is why large sparse-matrix libraries switched to 64-bit indices. (c) No: the gap at \(2^{53}\) is 2, so \(2^{53} + 1\) is a tie and rounds to \(2^{53}\) (round half to even). 2^53 + 1 - 2^53 returns 0.
